react-todo-reducer.title: A pure reducer for a todo list
react-todo-reducer.description:
`useReducer` asks you for one pure function, `(state, action) => nextState`. Write `todoReducer(state, action)`
for a todo list. `state` is an array of `{ id, text, done }`. **Never mutate `state` or its items**; return new
arrays/objects for whatever changed, and return the *same* `state` when nothing changes.

| `action.type` | other fields | behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `"added"` | `id`, `text` | append `{ id, text: text.trim(), done: false }`. Ignore it (return `state`) when the trimmed text is empty or the id already exists |
| `"toggled"` | `id` | flip `done` of that todo |
| `"renamed"` | `id`, `text` | set the trimmed text; if the trimmed text is empty, **remove** the todo instead |
| `"removed"` | `id` | drop that todo |
| `"clearedDone"` | | drop every todo with `done: true` |
| `"allToggled"` | | if every todo is done, mark all as not done; otherwise mark all as done |
| anything else | | return `state` |

**Example:** `todoReducer([{id:1,text:"tea",done:false}], {type:"toggled", id:1})` → `[{id:1,text:"tea",done:true}]`

guide.prereqs: `useReducer` (lesson *useReducer and impossible states*), array `map`/`filter`, object spread.
guide.intuition: A reducer is a pure lookup: given the old list and a description of what happened, compute the new list. Every case is one array expression: spread to append, `map` to change one item, `filter` to drop items.
hints: Start with `removed` and `clearedDone`: both are a single `filter`.
For `toggled`, `map` over the list and return `{ ...t, done: !t.done }` only for the matching id; return `t` itself for the rest.
`allToggled` needs one fact first: is every todo done already? Compute it once, then `map` every item to `done: !allDone`.
guide.brute_force: Deep-clone the whole state with `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(state))`, mutate the clone, return it. It works but copies every todo on every action, so `React.memo` rows can never skip a render.
guide.approach:
1. `switch` on `action.type`.
2. `added`: trim, reject blank or duplicate id, otherwise `[...state, newTodo]`.
3. `toggled`/`renamed`: `map`, replacing only the matching item with a spread copy. `renamed` with blank text becomes a `filter`.
4. `removed`/`clearedDone`: `filter`.
5. `allToggled`: `allDone = every(done)`, then map to `!allDone`.

**Dry run** `[{1,a,done},{2,b,open}]` + `allToggled`: `allDone` is false, so both become done. Run it again: `allDone` is true, so both become open.
guide.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) extra space per action: one pass over the list, sharing every untouched item.
guide.pitfalls: Using `push` or assigning `t.done = ...` mutates state React still holds. Forgetting `default: return state` makes unknown actions return `undefined`. `[].every(...)` is `true`, which is harmless here because mapping an empty list gives an empty list.
guide.follow_up: Add an `"undo"` action by keeping `{ past, present }` in state.

react-fetch-reducer.title: Loading, error and stale responses in one reducer
react-fetch-reducer.description:
A data-fetching component has four situations: nothing asked yet, waiting, got data, got an error. Model them with a
single `status` field so contradictory combinations (loading **and** error) cannot exist, and make the reducer ignore
responses that belong to an older request.

Write `fetchReducer(state, action)`. State shape: `{ status, data, error, requestId }` with
`status` one of `"idle" | "loading" | "success" | "error"`. The provided driver folds a list of actions starting from
`{ status: "idle", data: null, error: null, requestId: null }` and returns the final state.

| action | behaviour |
|---|---|
| `{type:"started", requestId}` | `status: "loading"`, remember `requestId`, clear `error`, **keep** the previous `data` (so the UI can show stale results while refreshing) |
| `{type:"succeeded", requestId, data}` | only when `status` is `"loading"` **and** `requestId` equals the remembered one: `status: "success"`, store `data`, `error: null`. Otherwise return `state` |
| `{type:"failed", requestId, error}` | same guard: `status: "error"`, store `error`, keep the previous `data`. Otherwise return `state` |
| `{type:"reset"}` | back to the initial state |
| anything else | return `state` |

**Example:** `started(1)`, `started(2)`, `succeeded(1, "old")`, `succeeded(2, "new")` → `{status:"success", data:"new", error:null, requestId:2}`
(the late answer to request 1 is dropped).

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Fetching data* and *useReducer and impossible states*.
guide.intuition: Two ideas. First, one `status` string replaces a pile of booleans, so the state can only be in a legal situation. Second, every request carries a ticket number; a response is accepted only if its ticket is the one currently being waited on.
hints: Compute one boolean up front: is this action the answer to the request we are waiting for?
`started` never needs the guard: a new request always wins and simply replaces the remembered id.
`succeeded` after `succeeded` with the same id must be ignored too, which is why the guard also checks `status === "loading"`.
guide.brute_force: Three independent `useState` calls (`isLoading`, `error`, `data`) updated in separate places. It is easy to forget one, and nothing stops an old response from overwriting a newer one.
guide.approach:
1. `current = state.status === "loading" && action.requestId === state.requestId`.
2. `started`: loading, new id, error cleared, data kept.
3. `succeeded`/`failed`: apply only when `current`.
4. `reset`: return a fresh initial object.

**Dry run:** `started(1)` → loading/1. `started(2)` → loading/2. `succeeded(1)` → id 1 ≠ 2, ignored. `succeeded(2,"new")` → success with `"new"`.
guide.pitfalls: Clearing `data` on `started` makes the list flash empty on every refresh. Checking only the id lets a duplicate response flip an error back to success. Mutating `state` instead of returning a new object means React sees no change.
guide.follow_up: In a component the same guard is usually an `ignore` flag or an `AbortController` in the effect cleanup.

react-derive-view.title: Derived state: compute, don't store
react-derive-view.description:
Anything that can be calculated from existing state should be calculated during render, not kept in a second
`useState` that has to be synchronised. Write the selector `deriveView(state)`.

`state` is `{ todos: [{ id, text, done }], filter, query }` where `filter` is `"all"`, `"active"` (not done) or
`"done"`, and `query` is a search string.

Return:

- `visibleIds`: ids of todos that pass the filter **and** whose text contains `query.trim()` ignoring case
  (an empty trimmed query matches everything), in the original order
- `total`: number of todos; `doneCount`; `remaining` (not done), all counted over **all** todos, not just the visible ones
- `allDone`: `true` when there is at least one todo and none remain
- `isEmpty`: `true` when `visibleIds` is empty
- `label`: `"1 item left"` or `"N items left"` using `remaining`

**Example:** todos `[{1,"Tea",done},{2,"Milk",open}]`, filter `"active"`, query `""` →
`{visibleIds:[2], total:2, doneCount:1, remaining:1, allDone:false, isEmpty:false, label:"1 item left"}`

guide.prereqs: Lesson *State with useState* (the section on derived values).
guide.intuition: The only real state is the list, the chosen filter and the search text. Counts, labels and the visible rows are *views* of that state, so a plain function can produce them on every render.
hints: Normalise the query once: `query.trim().toLowerCase()`.
Count `doneCount` over all todos; `remaining` is `total - doneCount`.
`"".includes("")` is true for every string, so an empty query needs no special case.
guide.brute_force: Keep `visibleTodos`, `remaining` and `label` each in their own `useState` and update them in every handler. Miss one handler and the footer lies about the list.
guide.approach:
1. Lower-case the trimmed query.
2. Filter by status, then by text, then map to ids.
3. Count done todos once.
4. Build the return object from those three numbers.

**Dry run:** `[Tea ✓, Milk ✗]`, filter `active`: status filter keeps Milk, query `""` keeps it, `visibleIds = [2]`; `doneCount = 1`, `remaining = 1`, label `1 item left`.
guide.complexity: O(n · m) time where m is the text length (substring search), O(n) space.
guide.pitfalls: Counting over the *visible* rows makes the footer change when the user types in the search box. `allDone` must be false for an empty list, otherwise an empty app shows the 'all finished' state.
guide.follow_up: Wrap the call in `useMemo` only if profiling shows the list is large enough to matter.

react-set-in.title: Immutable nested update: setIn
react-set-in.description:
React compares state by reference, so a nested change needs a **new object at every level on the path** while
everything off the path is reused as-is (structural sharing).

Write `setIn(state, path, value)`:

- `path` is an array of keys; strings address object keys and numbers address array indexes
- return a copy of `state` in which the location at `path` holds `value`
- copy only the containers along the path: arrays stay arrays, objects stay objects, and every sibling keeps its
  original reference
- if a container on the path is missing (or is not an object/array), create it: an array when the **next** key is a
  number, otherwise an object
- an empty path returns `value` itself
- `state` must not be modified

The provided driver calls your function and returns `{ updated, originalIntact, newRoot, siblingsShared }`, so
mutation and over-copying are both detected.

**Example:** `setIn({user:{name:"Ann", tags:["a"]}, theme:{dark:true}}, ["user","tags",1], "b")` →
`{user:{name:"Ann", tags:["a","b"]}, theme:{dark:true}}` and `theme` is the very same object as before.

guide.prereqs: Spread syntax, recursion, lesson *State with useState* (objects and arrays in state).
guide.intuition: Think of the path as a rope from the root to one leaf. Every knot on the rope gets replaced by a copy; everything hanging off the side is tied onto the copies unchanged.
hints: Recursion mirrors the path: handle the first key, then recurse into that child with the rest of the path.
Copy the current container with `slice()` for arrays and `{ ...obj }` for objects before writing into it.
When the current value is not a container, look at the type of the key you are about to write to decide between `[]` and `{}`.
guide.brute_force: Deep-clone everything and mutate the clone. Correct values, but every reference changes, so every memoised child re-renders and the cost is O(size of the whole state).
guide.approach:
1. Empty path → return `value`.
2. Split `path` into `key` and `rest`.
3. Shallow-copy the container (or create one).
4. `copy[key] = setIn(child, rest, value)`.
5. Return the copy.

**Dry run** `setIn({a:{b:1}, s:{t:1}}, ["a","b"], 2)`: copy root → `{a, s}`; recurse into `a` with `["b"]`: copy `{b:1}`, set `b` to `setIn(1, [], 2) = 2`. Result root and `a` are new objects, `s` is the old reference.
guide.complexity: O(depth × width of the copied containers) time and space; untouched subtrees cost nothing.
guide.pitfalls: Spreading an array into `{}` turns it into an object with numeric keys. Writing into `state` before copying mutates the original. Copying the root only (a shallow copy) still leaves nested objects shared *and mutated*.
guide.follow_up: Libraries such as Immer generate exactly these copies from code that looks like mutation.

react-list-ops.title: Immutable list operations
react-list-ops.description:
Lists in state are changed with non-mutating recipes. Write `applyListOp(list, op)` where `list` is an array of
objects that each have a unique `id`. Return a **new array**; never change `list` or the objects in it, and reuse
the original object for every item the operation does not touch.

| `op` | result |
|---|---|
| `{type:"insert", index, item}` | `item` placed at `index` (clamp `index` into `0..list.length`) |
| `{type:"remove", id}` | without the item that has this id |
| `{type:"update", id, patch}` | that item replaced by `{...item, ...patch}` |
| `{type:"move", from, to}` | the item at index `from` moved so that it ends up at index `to` (clamp `to` into `0..list.length-1`); if `from` is out of range the contents stay the same |

Unknown ids simply change nothing (still return a new array). The driver reports
`{ result, originalIntact, newArray, othersShared }`.

**Example:** `applyListOp([{id:1},{id:2},{id:3}], {type:"move", from:0, to:2})` → `[{id:2},{id:3},{id:1}]`

guide.prereqs: Array `slice`, `filter`, `map`, spread. Lesson *State with useState*.
guide.intuition: Each mutating array method has a non-mutating twin: `push` → spread, `splice` for delete → `filter`, assignment → `map`. A move is 'copy the array, then splice the copy'.
hints: `insert` is two slices with the new item between them.
`update` is a `map` that returns the same object for every non-matching id.
For `move`, `slice()` first; `splice` on that private copy is safe.
guide.brute_force: Clone every item on every operation. The values are right, but every row gets a new identity, so memoised rows always re-render and focus/animation state tied to identity can reset.
guide.approach:
Clamp indexes first, then apply the matching recipe.

**Dry run** move `from 0, to 2` on `[1,2,3]`: copy → `[1,2,3]`; remove index 0 → `[2,3]` holding `1`; insert at 2 → `[2,3,1]`.
guide.complexity: O(n) time and space per operation.
guide.pitfalls: `splice`, `sort` and `reverse` change the array they are called on. Splicing with a negative index counts from the end, which is why clamping matters. Cloning items you did not change defeats structural sharing.
guide.follow_up: Modern JavaScript adds `toSpliced`, `toSorted` and `with`, which return copies.

react-shallow-deep-equal.title: Shallow equal vs deep equal
react-shallow-deep-equal.description:
`React.memo`, `PureComponent` and many selector libraries compare props **shallowly**: one level of keys, each
value compared with `Object.is`. A deep comparison walks the whole structure instead.

Write `compareBoth(a, b)` returning `{ shallow, deep }`.

**shallow**

1. `Object.is(a, b)` → `true`
2. if either side is not a non-null object → `false`
3. an array and a plain object are never equal
4. otherwise: the same number of own keys, and for every key `Object.is(a[key], b[key])`

**deep**: the same, except step 4 compares the values recursively with the deep rule.

Inputs come from JSON, so two separately written objects are always different references, exactly like two object
literals created during two renders.

**Examples:** `compareBoth({a:1}, {a:1})` → `{shallow:true, deep:true}` ·
`compareBoth({a:{}}, {a:{}})` → `{shallow:false, deep:true}`

guide.prereqs: `Object.is`, `Object.keys`, recursion. Lesson *memo, useMemo and useCallback*.
guide.intuition: Both comparisons share one skeleton; they differ only in how the values under each key are compared: identity for shallow, the same function again for deep.
hints: Write one helper that takes the inner comparison as a parameter.
Check key *counts* as well as key values, or `{a:1}` will equal `{a:1, b:2}`.
`Array.isArray(x) !== Array.isArray(y)` separates `[]` from `{}`.
guide.brute_force: Compare `JSON.stringify` output. It breaks on key order, treats shallow like deep, and is far slower.
guide.approach:
1. `Object.is` fast path.
2. Reject non-objects and array/object mixes.
3. Compare key counts.
4. Every key present in both and passing the inner comparison.

**Dry run** `{a:{}}` vs `{a:{}}`: not identical, both objects, one key each. Shallow: `Object.is({}, {})` is false. Deep: recurse, two empty objects, zero keys, true.
guide.complexity: Shallow: O(k) for k keys. Deep: O(total nodes).
guide.pitfalls: `===` gets `NaN` wrong (never equal to itself); `Object.is` does not. Iterating only the left object's keys misses extra keys on the right.
guide.follow_up: This is why passing a fresh object or arrow function as a prop defeats `React.memo`.

react-batch-updates.title: Batching and the update queue
react-batch-updates.description:
Inside one event handler React does not re-render after each `setState` call. It collects the calls in a queue,
processes the queue once the handler has finished, and renders at most once.

Simulate that for a single number of state. `simulateEvents(initial, events)`: `events` is a list of handlers and
each handler is a list of calls made during that handler:

| call | React code it stands for | effect on the pending value |
|---|---|---|
| `{kind:"set", value}` | `setN(5)` | becomes `value` |
| `{kind:"addStale", n}` | `setN(count + n)` where `count` is the value **from the render the handler belongs to** | becomes `renderValue + n` |
| `{kind:"add", n}` | `setN(c => c + n)` | pending value `+ n` |
| `{kind:"mul", n}` | `setN(c => c * n)` | pending value `× n` |

Process a handler's calls in order starting from the current state. When the handler ends, commit the pending value.
If it differs from the previous state (`Object.is`), that is **one** render; if it is the same, React bails out and
there is no render.

Return `{ state, renders, history }` where `history` holds the committed state after each handler.

**Example:** `simulateEvents(0, [[{kind:"addStale",n:1},{kind:"addStale",n:1},{kind:"addStale",n:1}]])` →
`{state:1, renders:1, history:[1]}` (three calls, each computing `0 + 1`).

guide.prereqs: Lesson *State with useState* (state as a snapshot, updater functions) and *Render, commit and batching*.
guide.intuition: Within a handler there are two numbers: the frozen value the handler's closure saw, and the value the queue has worked out so far. Plain values built from the frozen number ignore the queue; updater functions read the queue.
hints: Save `renderValue = state` before looping over a handler's calls.
`addStale` uses `renderValue`; `add` and `mul` use the running `pending`.
Count a render only after the whole handler, and only when `Object.is` says the value changed.
guide.brute_force: Treat every call as an immediate assignment followed by a render. That is how many beginners imagine `setState`, and it gives 3 for the triple `addStale` example instead of 1.
guide.approach:
For each handler: `pending = state`; fold the calls; compare; commit.

**Dry run** state 1, calls `add 1`, `addStale 5`: pending 2 after the updater, then replaced by `1 + 5 = 6`. One render, state 6. Swap the order: `addStale 5` → 6, `add 1` → 7.
guide.pitfalls: Counting one render per call; forgetting the bail-out when the result equals the old state; using the running value for the stale form.
guide.follow_up: Since React 18 the same batching also applies inside promises, timeouts and native event listeners.

react-format-phone.title: Controlled input formatter with caret
react-format-phone.description:
A controlled input may rewrite what the user types. The awkward part is the caret: after React writes the formatted
text back, the caret has to sit where the user expects, not jump to the end.

Write `formatPhone(raw, caret)`:

- `raw` is the text the browser reports after a keystroke (it may contain anything); `caret` is the caret index in `raw`
- keep only digits, at most the first 10
- format progressively as `(AAA) BBB-CCCC`: `""` → `""`, `"5"` → `"(5"`, `"555"` → `"(555"`, `"5551"` → `"(555) 1"`,
  `"5551234"` → `"(555) 123-4"`
- new caret: count the digits in `raw` that are **left of** `caret` (capped at the number of digits kept); the new
  caret sits immediately after that many digits in the formatted value (0 when the count is 0)

Return `{ value, caret }`.

**Example:** `formatPhone("(555) 1234", 10)` → `{ value: "(555) 123-4", caret: 11 }`

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Lifting state and controlled components*; basic regular expressions.
guide.intuition: Punctuation comes and goes, digits do not. So describe the caret as 'after the k-th digit', reformat, and translate that description back into an index.
hints: Strip non-digits with `/\D/g` and cut to 10.
Build the value in three steps guarded by `digits.length > 0`, `> 3`, `> 6`.
Walk the formatted string counting digits until you have passed `before` of them; the index you stop at is the caret.
guide.brute_force: Always put the caret at the end. Fine when appending, infuriating when the user fixes a digit in the middle.
guide.approach:
1. Extract digits. 2. Format. 3. `before` = digits left of the caret in `raw`, capped. 4. Scan the formatted value.

**Dry run** `("(5955) 123-4567", 3)`: digits `59551234567` → first ten `5955123456` → `(595) 512-3456`. Left of index 3 in raw are `5`,`9` → `before = 2`. Scanning `(595…`: after the second digit the index is 3.
guide.pitfalls: Forgetting the cap means a caret past the tenth digit never terminates the scan. Keeping the caret index unchanged is wrong whenever punctuation is inserted before it.
guide.follow_up: In React you apply the caret in `useLayoutEffect` with `input.setSelectionRange(caret, caret)`.

react-form-machine.title: Form validation state machine
react-form-machine.description:
A sign-in form is a small state machine. Write `runForm(events)` that starts from

```
values: { email: "", password: "" }, touched: {}, status: "editing", formError: null, submitCount: 0
```

and processes the events in order.

**Validation** (always derived from `values`):
email `""` → `"Email is required"`; not matching `/^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/` → `"Email looks wrong"`;
password `""` → `"Password is required"`; fewer than 8 characters → `"Password needs 8+ characters"`.

**Events**

| event | rule |
|---|---|
| `{type:"change", field, value}` | ignored while `status` is `"submitting"` or `"success"`. Otherwise set the value, and the status becomes `"editing"` with `formError: null` |
| `{type:"blur", field}` | mark the field as touched (ignored after `"success"`) |
| `{type:"submit"}` | ignored while `"submitting"` or `"success"`. Otherwise `submitCount + 1` and `formError: null`; if there is any validation error the status is `"editing"`, else `"submitting"` |
| `{type:"resolve"}` | only while `"submitting"` → `"success"` |
| `{type:"reject", message}` | only while `"submitting"` → `"failed"` with `formError: message` |

Return `{ status, values, visibleErrors, formError, submitCount }`. `visibleErrors` contains the error of a field
only when the field has an error **and** (it was touched **or** `submitCount > 0`), so nobody is shouted at before
they have typed.

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Forms* and *useReducer and impossible states*.
guide.intuition: Keep the stored state minimal (values, touched, status, formError, submitCount) and derive errors from the values. Each event is then a guarded transition: check the status, produce the next state.
hints: Write `validate(values)` first and call it wherever errors are needed; do not store errors.
Compute `locked = status is submitting or success` at the top of the loop; three of the five events consult it.
`visibleErrors` is a filter over `validate(values)` using `touched` and `submitCount`.
guide.brute_force: Store `errors` in state and try to keep them updated in every branch. You will forget one, and stale errors appear.
guide.approach:
Loop over the events applying the table. At the end derive errors and filter them.

**Dry run:** valid values, `submit` → submitting (count 1). `change` → ignored. `submit` → ignored. `resolve` → success.
guide.pitfalls: Letting `resolve` succeed when nothing was submitted; accepting edits during submission (the request and the screen then disagree); showing every error on first paint.
guide.follow_up: React 19's `useActionState` gives you the pending flag and the last result of a form action without hand-rolling this.

react-create-element.title: createElement: build a virtual DOM tree
react-create-element.description:
JSX is syntax sugar for function calls that return plain objects. Write that function:
`createElement(type, props, ...children)` returns

```
{ type, key, props: { ...otherProps, children: [ ...normalised children ] } }
```

Rules:

- `props` may be `null`. `key` is taken **out of** props: `String(props.key)` when present, otherwise `null`
- children may be nested arrays (as produced by `list.map(...)`): flatten them completely
- `null`, `undefined`, `true` and `false` render nothing: drop them
- strings and numbers become text elements: `{ type: "TEXT", key: null, props: { nodeValue: String(value), children: [] } }`.
  Note that `0` and `""` are kept. Only the four values above are skipped
- anything else (an element object) is kept as it is
- `props.children` is always an array, possibly empty

The driver converts a JSON description into nested `createElement` calls.

**Example:** `createElement("p", {id: "x", key: 7}, "Hi ", null, 3)` →
`{type:"p", key:"7", props:{id:"x", children:[text("Hi "), text("3")]}}`

guide.prereqs: Rest/spread syntax, recursion. Lesson *JSX, components and props*.
guide.intuition: An element is a description, not a DOM node: a type, some props and its children. The only real work is tidying the children so later stages can treat them uniformly.
hints: Destructure `key` away from the rest of the props; remember `props` can be `null`.
Write a small recursive `add(child)` that handles arrays by calling itself on each entry.
Skip exactly four values: `null`, `undefined`, `true`, `false`. Test with `0`.
guide.brute_force: `children.flat().filter(Boolean)` flattens one level only and throws away `0` and `""`. The same mistake in JSX (`{count && <Badge/>}`) is why a stray `0` shows up on screen: React itself keeps numbers.
guide.approach:
1. Split props into `key` and the rest.
2. Walk the children depth-first, pushing text elements and element objects.
3. Return the element with `children` overriding any `children` that came in through props.

**Dry run** `("p", {key:7}, "Hi ", null, 3)`: key `"7"`; children → text `Hi `, skip `null`, text `3`.
guide.complexity: O(number of children including nested arrays).
guide.pitfalls: Treating key `0` as missing; dropping `0` children; leaving `key` inside props (React never passes it to the component).
guide.follow_up: Real React also records `ref`, the owner and a `$$typeof` marker that blocks JSON-injected elements.

react-render-to-string.title: Render a virtual tree to an HTML string
react-render-to-string.description:
Server rendering turns the element tree into HTML text. Write `renderToString(node)`. **Nodes** - `null`, `true`, `false` → `""` - a string or number → its text with `&`, `<`, `>` escaped as `&`, `<`, `>` - an array → the concatenation of its items - `{ type, props }` → an element. `props.children` may be missing, a single node or an array - type `"Fragment"` renders only its children **Attributes**, in the order the props appear: - skip `children`, `key`, `ref`, and any prop whose value is `null` or `false` - `className` is written as `class`, `htmlFor` as `for` - value `true` → the bare name (` disabled`) - `style` given as an object → `style="font-size:12px;color:red"`: camelCase names become kebab-case, pairs are joined with `;`, values are used as they are - everything else → ` name="value"` with `&`, `<`, `>` and `"` (`"`) escaped **Void elements** `br`, `hr`, `img`, `input`, `meta`, `link` are written as `
` (attributes allowed, never children). Other elements are `children`. **Example:** `{type:"a", props:{href:"/x?a=1&b=2", className:"link", children:["Tom & ", {type:"b", props:{children:"Jerry"}}]}}` → `Tom & Jerry`

guide.prereqs: Recursion over trees; lesson *The virtual DOM and reconciliation*.
guide.intuition: Rendering to a string is a post-order walk: render the children to text, then wrap that text in the element's opening and closing tags. Escaping is what keeps data from becoming markup.
hints: Handle the four non-element cases first (nothing, text, array, fragment).
Build the attribute string in a loop over `Object.keys(props)` with a `continue` for the skipped names and values.
Escape `&` before `<` and `>`, otherwise you double-escape your own entities.
guide.brute_force: Concatenate values without escaping. It looks right until a user names themselves `<script>`, at which point you have built a cross-site scripting hole.
guide.approach:
1. Leaf cases. 2. Render children. 3. Fragment → children only. 4. Attributes with renames, booleans and style. 5. Void elements self-close. **Dry run** `{type:"p", props:{style:{fontSize:"12px"}, children:0}}`: children `0` → `"0"`; style → `font-size:12px`; result `

0

`.
guide.complexity: O(size of the tree + length of the output).
guide.pitfalls: `if (!node) return ""` silently drops the number `0`. Booleans as attributes need the bare-name form. Void elements must not get a closing tag.
guide.follow_up: Hydration is the reverse trip: React walks existing HTML and attaches event handlers instead of creating nodes.

react-keyed-list-diff.title: Keyed list diff: which children move?
react-keyed-list-diff.description:
When a list re-renders, React matches old and new children by `key` and works out the DOM operations. Implement the
same single-pass strategy React uses. `diffKeys(oldKeys, newKeys)` (both arrays of unique strings) returns

```
{ remove: [keys], insert: [{ key, index }], move: [{ key, index }] }
```

- `remove`: keys in the old list that are missing from the new one, in old order
- walk the new list from left to right keeping `lastPlacedIndex` (start at `-1`), the largest **old index** of any
  reused child so far:
  - a key that did not exist before → `insert` with its new index
  - a reused key whose old index is **less than** `lastPlacedIndex` → `move` with its new index
  - otherwise it stays where it is and `lastPlacedIndex` becomes its old index

**Examples**

`diffKeys(["a","b","c"], ["a","c","b"])` → `{remove:[], insert:[], move:[{key:"b", index:2}]}`

`diffKeys(["a","b","c","d"], ["d","a","b","c"])` → three moves (`a`, `b`, `c`): moving the last item to the front
is the worst case for this strategy, although a human would move only `d`.

guide.prereqs: `Map`/`Set`; lessons *Lists, keys and events* and *The virtual DOM and reconciliation*.
guide.intuition: Reused children that already appear in increasing old-index order can stay put. `lastPlacedIndex` is the high-water mark of that increasing run; anything that used to sit before the mark has been overtaken and must be moved after it.
hints: Build `key → old index` once so lookups are O(1).
Update `lastPlacedIndex` only when the child stays; a moved child does not raise the mark.
Removals are independent of the walk: filter the old keys by membership in the new set.
guide.brute_force: Flag every child whose index changed. Inserting one row at the top would then 'move' the entire list, the very cost keys exist to avoid.
guide.approach:
**Dry run** old `[a,b,c,d]`, new `[d,a,b,c]`: `d` old 3 ≥ −1 → stays, mark 3. `a` old 0 < 3 → move. `b` 1 < 3 → move. `c` 2 < 3 → move.

Reverse case new `[b,c,d,a]`: `b` stays (mark 1), `c` stays (2), `d` stays (3), `a` 0 < 3 → one move.
guide.pitfalls: Raising the mark for moved children (the second wrong solution) under-counts moves in reversals. Comparing against the new index instead of old indices confuses 'shifted because of an insert' with 'moved'.
guide.follow_up: Finding the *minimum* number of moves needs the longest increasing subsequence, which some other frameworks compute.

react-vdom-diff.title: Diff two virtual trees into patches
react-vdom-diff.description:
Write `diff(oldTree, newTree)` that returns the list of patches turning the old tree into the new one.

A node is either a **string** (text) or `{ type, props, children }` (`props` is an object of primitives, `children`
an array; either may be missing, meaning empty). Children are matched **by position** (no keys here).
A `path` is the list of child indexes from the root (`[]` is the root itself).

Compare two nodes at `path`:

1. both strings: if different emit `{op:"TEXT", path, value: newText}`
2. one is a string and the other is not, or the `type` differs: emit `{op:"REPLACE", path, node: newNode}` and do
   **not** look inside
3. same type:
   1. for each prop name of the new node in **alphabetical** order whose value differs from the old one (or is new):
      `{op:"SET_PROP", path, name, value}`
   2. for each prop name of the old node in alphabetical order that the new node lacks: `{op:"REMOVE_PROP", path, name}`
   3. recurse into the children present in both, in index order, at `[...path, i]`
   4. for each extra new child, in order: `{op:"APPEND", path, node}`
   5. for each extra old child, **from the last index down**: `{op:"REMOVE_CHILD", path, index}`

Return the patches in exactly the order they are produced.

**Example:** old `{type:"p", props:{id:"a"}, children:["hi"]}`, new `{type:"p", props:{id:"b"}, children:["yo", "!"]}` →
`[{op:"SET_PROP",path:[],name:"id",value:"b"}, {op:"TEXT",path:[0],value:"yo"}, {op:"APPEND",path:[],node:"!"}]`

guide.prereqs: Tree recursion; lesson *The virtual DOM and reconciliation*.
guide.intuition: React's two heuristics in miniature: a different type means 'throw the subtree away', the same type means 'keep the node, update its attributes, then compare children pairwise'.
hints: Decide the three cases (text/text, replace, same type) before touching props.
Sort the prop names so the output order is deterministic.
Removing children from the end means earlier indexes stay valid while the patches are applied.
guide.brute_force: Replace the root whenever anything differs. Always correct, but it destroys input focus, scroll position and every child's state, and does maximal DOM work.
guide.approach:
Recursive `walk(a, b, path)` pushing onto one shared array, following the numbered rules in order.

**Dry run** (example): same type `p`; prop `id` differs → SET_PROP. Children: index 0 `hi` vs `yo` → TEXT at `[0]`. New has one extra child → APPEND `!`.
guide.complexity: O(n) in the number of nodes compared; a replaced subtree is not visited.
guide.pitfalls: Recursing into a replaced node emits patches for nodes that no longer exist. Removing children front-to-back shifts the remaining indexes. The index-based matching makes a prepend rewrite every row (see the test with `z`), which is the motivation for keys.
guide.follow_up: Extend the node shape with `key` and reuse your `diffKeys` to emit MOVE patches.

react-hooks-runtime.title: A tiny hooks runtime
react-hooks-runtime.description:
Hooks are not magic: React keeps an array of slots per component and a cursor that advances on every hook call,
which is why hooks must be called in the same order on every render.

Write `createRuntime()` returning `{ useState, useEffect, render, flush, unmount }` for **one** component instance.

- `useState(initial)` → `[value, setValue]`. The slot is created on the first render only.
  `setValue(next)` accepts a value or an updater function `(previous) => next` (applied to the latest queued value).
  If the result differs from the stored value (`Object.is`) store it and mark the runtime **dirty**; it never renders
  by itself
- `useEffect(fn, deps)` registers an effect. It is **scheduled** for this render when it is the first render, when
  `deps` is not an array, or when any dependency differs from last time (`Object.is`, also when the length differs)
- `render(component, props)` resets the cursor, clears the dirty flag, calls `component(props)`, then (the "commit")
  first runs the previous cleanup of **every** scheduled effect, in hook order, then runs every scheduled effect in
  hook order, storing a returned function as its cleanup
- `flush()`: if dirty, render again with the same component and props and return `true`; otherwise return `false`
- `unmount()`: run all remaining cleanups in hook order and forget everything

The provided driver defines a `Counter` component with two state hooks and three effects (`[count]`, `[]`, no array),
runs a script of actions and returns the log. Read the driver carefully: it is the specification of what gets logged.

**Example:** `[["render","A"],["inc"],["inc"],["flush"]]` →
`["render:A:0:a","effect:count=0","effect:mount","effect:always","render:A:2:a","cleanup:count=0","effect:count=2","effect:always","flush:true"]`

guide.prereqs: Closures; lessons *State with useState*, *useEffect* and *Render, commit and batching*.
guide.intuition: State lives outside the component function in an array. Each render replays the hook calls in order, so call number *i* always finds slot *i*. Effects are just callbacks remembered during render and executed after it.
hints: Start with `useState` and `render` only; get `render:A:0:a` logged, then make `inc` + `flush` log `render:A:1:a`.
In `useEffect`, do not run anything. Push `{ slot, fn }` onto a per-render list when the deps changed.
`render` needs two loops over that list: all old cleanups first, then all new effects.
guide.brute_force: Run every effect after every render and ignore dependencies. Correct for effects without an array, wrong for `[]` (the 'mount' effect would resubscribe on every render).
guide.approach:
1. `hooks[]`, `cursor`, `dirty`, `current`, `pending`.
2. `useState`: slot by cursor; setter resolves updater, compares, stores, sets dirty.
3. `useEffect`: compare deps, queue.
4. `render`: reset, call, cleanups, effects.
5. `flush`/`unmount`.

**Dry run** of the example: first render logs the render line, then three effects. `inc` twice → value 2, dirty. `flush` renders (`render:A:2:a`); `[count]` changed 0→2 so its cleanup (captured `0`) runs, then `effect:count=2`; `[]` is skipped; the array-less effect runs; finally the driver logs `flush:true`.
guide.pitfalls: Applying the updater to the initial value instead of the latest one; running an effect's cleanup immediately before its own effect instead of all cleanups first; forgetting that the cleanup closes over the *old* render's values; not resetting the cursor.
guide.follow_up: Calling a hook inside an `if` would shift every later slot. Try it in the driver and watch state swap places.

react-deps-changed.title: Should the effect run again?
react-deps-changed.description:
After every render React decides, per effect, whether to run it again. Write `depsChanged(prev, next)`:

- `next` is not an array (the effect was written without a dependency array) → `true`
- `prev` is not an array (first render) → `true`
- different lengths → `true`
- otherwise `true` when at least one position differs according to `Object.is`, else `false`

`Object.is` is like `===` except that `NaN` equals `NaN` and `0` does not equal `-0`. Objects, arrays and functions
are compared by reference, so two look-alike literals are different.

The driver lets the JSON tests express awkward values: `"$NaN"`, `"$-0"`, and `"$ref:name"` (the same object each
time the same name is used).

**Examples:** `([1,"a"], [1,"a"])` → `false` · `([{}], [{}])` → `true` · `(["$ref:u"], ["$ref:u"])` → `false`

guide.prereqs: Lesson *useEffect and its dependency rules*.
guide.intuition: The dependency array is compared slot by slot with identity semantics. Nothing looks inside objects.
hints: Two early returns cover 'no array' and 'first render'.
Use `Object.is`, not `===`.
`some` returns `false` for an empty array, which is exactly the `[]` case: never changed.
guide.brute_force: Stringify both arrays and compare. It claims `[{}]` equals `[{}]` (React says changed) and cannot represent functions at all.
guide.approach:
Guard, guard, length, `some`.

**Dry run** `([0], [-0])`: arrays, same length, `Object.is(-0, 0)` is false → changed.
guide.pitfalls: `===` reports `NaN` as changed forever, which would loop an effect whose dependency is `NaN`.
guide.follow_up: The same comparison drives `useMemo` and `useCallback`.

react-stale-closure.title: Predict the stale closure
react-stale-closure.description:
A component shows a counter that starts at `0`. A button increments it (`onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}`,
always created fresh, so a click always sees the latest render). An effect with an **empty dependency array**
starts an interval once, at mount. The interval callback is written in one of three ways:

| `mode` | interval callback | what it sees |
|---|---|---|
| `"stale"` | `setCount(count + 1)` | `count` from the **first** render, forever `0` |
| `"updater"` | `setCount(c => c + 1)` | the latest state, supplied by React |
| `"ref"` | `setCount(latest.current + 1)` where `latest.current = count` is assigned on every render | the latest rendered value |

There is also a "remind me" button: `onClick={() => setTimeout(() => log(count), 3000)}`. In `"stale"` and
`"updater"` mode the timeout logs the `count` of the render in which the button was clicked. In `"ref"` mode it is
written as `log(latest.current)` and logs the value current when the timeout fires.

Write `simulate(mode, events)`. Each event is one of `"click"`, `"tick"` (the interval fires), `"snapshot"` (the
remind-me button is clicked) or `"fire"` (all pending timeouts run, oldest first). Assume a re-render completes
after every event.

Return `{ counts, logged }`: the counter after each event, and every value logged by the timeouts.

**Example:** `simulate("stale", ["click","click","tick","click"])` → `{ counts: [1,2,1,2], logged: [] }`

guide.prereqs: Closures; lessons *useEffect* and *React interview essentials: renders, keys and closures*.
guide.intuition: Every render is a snapshot with its own `count` constant. A function keeps the snapshot it was created in. The interval callback was created once, in the first snapshot; the click handler is recreated every render.
hints: In stale mode a tick does not add one to the current count. It *sets* the count to `0 + 1`.
A snapshot stores a function. Decide at creation time whether it captures a number or reads the ref later.
Update `latest.current` after every event, mirroring the assignment during render.
guide.brute_force: Assume every callback sees current state (first wrong solution). That is how the code *reads*, and it is exactly the bug.
guide.approach:
Track `count`, a ref object and a queue of timeout closures.

**Dry run** stale, `click, click, tick, click`: 1, 2, then tick sets `0 + 1 = 1`, then click sees 1 → 2.
guide.pitfalls: Forgetting that in updater mode the *timeout* is still a snapshot: the updater form fixes writes, not reads.
guide.follow_up: The lint rule `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` would flag the stale version: `count` is used but not listed.

react-memo-shallow.title: memo: skip renders with shallow props
react-memo-shallow.description:
`React.memo(Component)` returns a component that re-uses its **last** output when the new props are shallowly equal
to the previous props.

Write `memo(render)`. It returns a function `(props) => output` that

- calls `render(props)` the first time
- on later calls compares `props` with the props of the **previous call** (not all earlier calls): same set of own
  keys and `Object.is` for every value
- if equal, returns the remembered output without calling `render`; otherwise calls `render`, remembers the new
  props and output

The driver wraps a component that returns `"render#N"` (N counts real renders) and feeds it a list of props objects.
A prop value `"$ref:name"` stands for one shared object per name; any other object in the JSON is a brand-new
reference each time, like an inline `{}` or `() => {}` in JSX.

**Example:** `[{id:1},{id:1},{id:2},{id:1}]` → `["render#1","render#1","render#2","render#3"]`

guide.prereqs: Problem *Shallow equal vs deep equal*; lesson *memo, useMemo and useCallback*.
guide.intuition: A one-entry cache keyed by 'the props I saw last time'. The comparison is cheap on purpose: one pass over the keys, identity per value.
hints: Keep three variables in the closure: whether there is a previous call, its props, its output.
Compare key counts first, then each key with `Object.is`.
Only the previous call matters. `A, B, A` renders three times.
guide.brute_force: A deep comparison (or JSON) on every call. It skips more renders but can cost more than the render it saves, and it is wrong for functions.
guide.approach: **Dry run** `[{user:{…}}, {user:{…}}]` with inline objects: second call has the same keys but `Object.is(obj1, obj2)` is false → render again. With `$ref:ann` both calls hold the same reference → skipped.
guide.complexity: O(k) per call for k props.
guide.pitfalls: Iterating only the previous keys misses a newly added prop. A history cache is not what React does and would leak memory.
guide.follow_up: `React.memo(Component, arePropsEqual)` lets you replace the comparison; `useMemo`/`useCallback` exist to keep object and function props referentially stable so this check can succeed.

react-event-delegation.title: Event delegation: capture and bubble
react-event-delegation.description:
React attaches one native listener per event type at the root and then **simulates** propagation through the
component tree itself. Reproduce that.

`dispatchEvent(tree, targetId, type)`:

- a node is `{ id, on: { ... }, children: [ ... ] }` (`on` and `children` may be missing)
- handlers are stored under the event name: `on.click` for the bubble phase and `on.clickCapture` for the capture phase
- find the path from the root to the node whose id is `targetId` (ids are unique). If there is none return `[]`
- **capture phase:** from the root down to the target, call each `typeCapture` handler
- **bubble phase:** from the target back up to the root, call each `type` handler
- calling a handler appends `"id:capture"` or `"id:bubble"` to the log. A handler whose value is `"stop"` also calls
  `stopPropagation()`: nothing after it runs (in either phase). Any other truthy value just logs

Return the log.

**Example:** root `app` (`click: "log"`) → `list` (`clickCapture: "log"`) → `item` (`click: "log"`), target `item`,
type `"click"` → `["list:capture", "item:bubble", "app:bubble"]`

guide.prereqs: DOM event propagation; lesson *Lists, keys and events*.
guide.intuition: Propagation is two walks over one list: the ancestors of the target, root first for capture and reversed for bubble.
hints: A depth-first search that pushes on the way down and pops on failure leaves exactly the ancestor path in the array.
Write one helper that looks up a handler, logs, and reports whether propagation should stop.
Stopping in the capture phase must skip the entire bubble phase.
guide.brute_force: Visit every node that has a handler. Siblings and descendants of the target must never fire.
guide.approach: **Dry run** (example): path `[app, list, item]`. Capture: `app` none, `list` logs, `item` none. Bubble: `item` logs, `list` none, `app` logs.
guide.complexity: O(n) to find the target, O(depth) to dispatch.
guide.pitfalls: Bubbling in root-to-target order; ignoring `stop` during capture; firing handlers of a different event type.
guide.follow_up: Since React 17 the single native listener sits on the root container, not on `document`, so several React roots can coexist.

react-context-lookup.title: Context: find the nearest provider
react-context-lookup.description:
`useContext(SomeContext)` returns the value of the **closest provider above** the calling component, or the
context's default when there is none.

`resolveContext(tree, targetId, name, fallback)`:

- a node is `{ id, provides: { contextName: value }, children: [...] }` (`provides` and `children` optional)
- a node's `provides` applies to its **descendants only**, not to itself (a component that renders a provider does
  not read that provider's value)
- return `{ found: true, value }` for the node with id `targetId`: the value from the nearest ancestor that
  provides `name`, else `fallback`
- a provider may provide `null`; that still counts as provided
- unknown `targetId` → `{ found: false, value: null }`

**Example:** `app` provides `theme: "light"`; its child `sidebar` provides `theme: "dark"`; `sidebar`'s child `button`
→ `"dark"`; `app`'s other child `main` → `"light"`; `sidebar` itself → `"light"`; `app` itself → the fallback.

guide.prereqs: Tree traversal; lesson *Context and global state*.
guide.intuition: Pass the 'current value' down as a parameter while you walk the tree. Each provider swaps the value for its subtree only; siblings never see it.
hints: Give the recursive function a second parameter: the value inherited from above.
Check for the target *before* applying the node's own `provides`.
Use `hasOwnProperty` (or `in`), not truthiness, so `null` and `false` values count.
guide.brute_force: Find the path to the target first, then scan the path backwards for a provider. Equally correct, two passes.
guide.approach: **Dry run** target `button`: visit `app` with `system`; not the target; children inherit `light`. Visit `sidebar` with `light`; children inherit `dark`. Visit `button` with `dark` → found.
guide.pitfalls: Using `||` drops falsy provided values; applying a node's provider to itself.
guide.follow_up: When a provider's value changes, every consumer below it re-renders, which is why big frequently-changing objects make poor context values.

react-debounce-search.title: Debounced search controller
react-debounce-search.description:
A search box should not hit the server on every keystroke. *Debouncing* means: wait until the user has been quiet for
`delay` milliseconds, then search once. Timers are hard to test, so here time is explicit.

`debounceLog(events, delay)`: `events` is sorted by timestamp `t` (milliseconds) and each is one of

- `{t, type:"input", value}`: the user changed the text. Replace any pending search with one due at `t + delay`
- `{t, type:"flush"}`: the user pressed Enter. If a search is pending, run it **now** (at `t`)
- `{t, type:"cancel"}`: the box was cleared/unmounted. Drop the pending search

Rules:

- before handling an event at time `t`, a pending search whose due time is `<= t` runs first (at its due time)
- after the last event, a still-pending search runs at its due time
- "running" a search means: take the pending value, trim it; if it equals the query of the **last search that ran**
  (initially `""`), do nothing; otherwise record `{t, query}` and remember it

Return the recorded searches.

**Example:** delay 300, inputs `"r"`@0, `"re"`@100, `"rea"`@250, `"react"`@900 → `[{t:550, query:"rea"}, {t:1200, query:"react"}]`

guide.prereqs: `setTimeout`/`clearTimeout`; lesson *Interview builds: debounced search, modal, infinite scroll*.
guide.intuition: There is at most one pending timer. Every keystroke throws the old timer away and starts a new one. With explicit timestamps, 'the timer fired' becomes 'its due time is not later than the next event'.
hints: Keep `pending = { value, due }` or `null`.
At the top of each loop iteration, settle a pending search that is already due.
Put the trim-and-deduplicate logic in one `run(t)` helper used by due timers, flushes and the final drain.
guide.brute_force: Search on every input event. Twenty keystrokes become twenty requests whose responses can arrive out of order.
guide.approach: **Dry run** (example, delay 300): `r`@0 → due 300. `re`@100: 300 > 100, replace → due 400. `rea`@250 → due 550. `react`@900: 550 ≤ 900 → run at 550 with `rea`; new pending due 1200. End: run at 1200.
guide.pitfalls: Keeping the old due time when a new input arrives turns debounce into throttle. Using `<` instead of `<=` loses a search that is due exactly when the next key arrives. Forgetting to drain after the loop.
guide.follow_up: In a component the cleanup function of `useEffect` plays the role of `cancel`.

react-paginate.title: Pagination maths
react-paginate.description:
Write `paginate(items, page, pageSize)` for client-side pagination. Pages are numbered from 1 and `pageSize >= 1`.

Return

- `totalPages`: `ceil(items.length / pageSize)`, but at least `1` (an empty list still has one empty page)
- `page`: the requested page clamped into `1..totalPages`
- `items`: the slice for that page
- `hasPrev`, `hasNext`
- `total`: `items.length`
- `from`, `to`: 1-based positions of the first and last item shown (`0` and `0` when the page is empty), for a
  "Showing 11–20 of 45" label

**Example:** `paginate(["a","b","c","d","e"], 2, 2)` →
`{items:["c","d"], page:2, totalPages:3, hasPrev:true, hasNext:true, total:5, from:3, to:4}`

guide.prereqs: `Array.prototype.slice`, integer division. Lesson *Sorting, searching, pagination and optimistic updates*.
guide.intuition: Everything follows from one number: the index of the first item on the page, `(page − 1) × pageSize`.
hints: Compute `totalPages` first, then clamp the page.
`slice` never throws for out-of-range indexes, it returns fewer items.
`to = start + slice.length` handles the short last page.
guide.brute_force: Chunk the whole list into pages on every render and index into the chunks: O(n) work where O(pageSize) is enough.
guide.approach: **Dry run** 5 items, page 9, size 2: `totalPages = 3`, page clamps to 3, start 4, slice `[e]`, from 5, to 5, no next.
guide.pitfalls: `floor(n / size) + 1` gives an extra empty page when n divides evenly. Not clamping leaves the user on page 9 of 3 after a filter shrinks the list.
guide.follow_up: Server pagination returns `total` (or a cursor) with each page; the same maths drives the buttons.

react-page-window.title: Page buttons with ellipses
react-page-window.description:
A pager for 50 pages cannot show 50 buttons. Write `pageWindow(current, total, siblings)` returning what to render:
page numbers and the string `"..."` for gaps.

- `total <= 0` → `[]`. Clamp `current` into `1..total`
- always include page `1`, page `total`, and every page from `current - siblings` to `current + siblings` that exists
- list them in increasing order; between two listed pages that are not adjacent:
  - if exactly **one** page is missing, show that page (an ellipsis would take the same room)
  - otherwise show `"..."`

**Examples:** `pageWindow(5, 10, 1)` → `[1, "...", 4, 5, 6, "...", 10]` ·
`pageWindow(3, 10, 1)` → `[1, 2, 3, 4, "...", 10]`

guide.prereqs: Sets, sorting numbers. Lesson *Sorting, searching, pagination and optimistic updates*.
guide.intuition: Decide *which* pages are shown first, as a set. Formatting the gaps is then a single pass over the sorted set.
hints: A `Set` removes the duplicates when the window touches page 1 or the last page.
Sort numerically: the default sort compares strings, so 10 lands before 2.
Track the previously emitted page; the gap size `p - previous` decides between nothing, a number and `...`.
guide.brute_force: Hand-written branches for 'near the start', 'near the end' and 'middle'. Works until `siblings` or `total` changes.
guide.approach:
**Dry run** `(3, 10, 1)`: set `{1,10,2,3,4}` → sorted `1,2,3,4,10`. Gaps: none until `4 → 10` (6 apart) → `...`.

`(4, 10, 1)`: set `{1,10,3,4,5}`; `1 → 3` is a gap of exactly one page, so show `2`.
guide.pitfalls: Showing `1 ... 3` (an ellipsis hiding a single page); unsorted or string-sorted output; not clamping `current`.
guide.follow_up: Render the numbers as buttons with `aria-current="page"` on the active one and the ellipsis as plain text.

react-sort-table.title: Sortable table: header clicks and stable order
react-sort-table.description:
A table sorts by the column whose header was clicked. Write `sortTable(rows, clicks)`.

**Sort state** starts as `{ key: null, dir: "asc" }` (unsorted). For each column name in `clicks`:

- a different column than the current `key` → `{ key: column, dir: "asc" }`
- the same column, currently `"asc"` → `"desc"`
- the same column, currently `"desc"` → back to unsorted `{ key: null, dir: "asc" }`

**Ordering** for the final state (never modify `rows`):

- unsorted → the original order
- compare the values under `key`: numbers numerically, strings **ignoring case**
- rows whose value is `null` or missing go **last in both directions**
- ties keep their original relative order in both directions (a *stable* sort)

Return `{ sort: { key, dir }, rows: sortedRows }`.

**Example:** rows `[{n:"bob",age:30},{n:"Al",age:25},{n:"cy",age:null}]`, clicks `["n"]` → order `Al, bob, cy`;
clicks `["age","age"]` → order `bob (30), Al (25), cy (null)`.

guide.prereqs: `Array.prototype.sort` with a comparator. Lesson *Sorting, searching, pagination and optimistic updates*.
guide.intuition: Two separate problems: a three-state toggle (the *state*) and a comparator (the *derived* view). The sorted rows are never stored; they are recomputed from rows + sort state.
hints: Replay the clicks with two variables, `key` and `dir`.
Decorate each row with its original index so the comparator can break ties explicitly.
Handle missing values before looking at the direction, so they sink in both directions.
guide.brute_force: Sort ascending then `reverse()` for descending. Reversal also reverses ties and floats the empty values to the top.
guide.approach: **Dry run** clicks `[age, age]`: unsorted → age/asc → age/desc. Compare 30 vs 25 descending → 30 first; `null` last.
guide.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.
guide.pitfalls: Sorting `rows` in place mutates props/state. Comparing mixed-case strings with `<` puts every capital before every lower-case letter. A two-state toggle never lets the user return to the natural order.
guide.follow_up: `Intl.Collator` gives locale-aware comparison (accents, numeric strings).

react-route-matcher.title: Route matcher with params
react-route-matcher.description:
A client-side router maps the address bar to a component. Write `matchRoute(routes, path)`.

`routes` is a list of pattern strings. A pattern is made of `/`-separated segments:

- a **static** segment such as `users` matches only that exact text
- a **param** such as `:id` matches exactly one segment and captures it under that name
- a **splat** `*` (only allowed as the last segment) matches the rest of the path, **including nothing**, and captures
  it (joined with `/`) under the name `"*"`

Before matching, drop anything from `?` onwards in `path` and ignore empty segments (so `/users/7/` equals `/users/7`).
Captured values are passed through `decodeURIComponent`.

When several patterns match, rank them: give every pattern a score list with one entry per pattern segment
(static 3, param 2, splat 1). Compare the lists left to right; the first difference decides (higher wins). If one
list is a prefix of the other, the **shorter** wins. If still tied, the earlier pattern in `routes` wins.

Return `{ pattern, params }` or `null`.

**Example:** routes `["/users/:id", "/users/new", "/*"]`, path `/users/new` → `{pattern:"/users/new", params:{}}`;
path `/users/42?tab=a` → `{pattern:"/users/:id", params:{id:"42"}}`; path `/nope/x` → `{pattern:"/*", params:{"*":"nope/x"}}`

guide.prereqs: String splitting; lesson *Routing with React Router*.
guide.intuition: Matching is a segment-by-segment comparison; ranking says 'the more literal the pattern, the better', so `/users/new` beats `/users/:id` no matter which was declared first.
hints: Normalise both sides with the same `split` helper.
While matching, push 3, 2 or 1 onto a score array.
A pattern without a splat must consume exactly as many segments as the path has.
guide.brute_force: Return the first pattern that matches. Then the order of the route table silently decides behaviour, and a catch-all listed first swallows everything.
guide.approach: **Dry run** `/users/new` against `/users/:id` → score `[3,2]`; against `/users/new` → `[3,3]` wins; `/*` → `[1]` loses at position 0.
guide.pitfalls: Forgetting to strip the query string; a splat that requires at least one segment; summing scores (then a long param-only pattern can beat a short static one).
guide.follow_up: React Router ranks nested route branches with a similar scoring idea.

react-optimistic-update.title: Optimistic updates with rollback
react-optimistic-update.description:
An *optimistic* UI shows the result of an action before the server confirms it. The robust design keeps two things:
the last **confirmed** data and a queue of **pending** operations. What the user sees is always "confirmed data with
the pending operations replayed on top". A failure then needs no special undo: remove the operation and recompute.

`runOptimistic(initial, events)`: `initial` maps item id → like count (the confirmed data). Events:

- `{type:"mutate", reqId, id, delta}`: the user clicked. Queue the operation (ignore it when `id` is not in the
  confirmed data or `reqId` is already pending)
- `{type:"ok", reqId}`: the server accepted it. Apply its delta to the confirmed data and remove it from the queue
- `{type:"fail", reqId}`: the server rejected it. Remove it from the queue
- `{type:"refetch", data}`: fresh confirmed data arrived (same shape as `initial`). Pending operations stay queued

Unknown `reqId`s are ignored. When replaying or confirming, skip operations whose id is not present in the
confirmed data.

After **every** event record `{ view, pending }`: `view` is the id → count map the user sees, `pending` the queued
`reqId`s in order. Return the list of records.

**Example:** initial `{a:10}`; `mutate r1 +1`, `mutate r2 +1`, `fail r1`, `ok r2` → views `{a:11}`, `{a:12}`, `{a:11}`, `{a:11}`.

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Sorting, searching, pagination and optimistic updates*.
guide.intuition: Do not edit the displayed data and then try to un-edit it. Keep truth and guesses apart, and derive the display: `view = replay(pending, confirmed)`. Rollback becomes deletion.
hints: Two variables: `confirmed` (object) and `pending` (array of operations).
`ok` moves an operation's effect from the queue into the confirmed data; `fail` only removes it.
Build the view after every event by copying `confirmed` and applying each pending delta.
guide.brute_force: Snapshot the view on each click and restore the snapshot on failure. With two overlapping requests, restoring the first snapshot also erases the second (still valid) click.
guide.approach: **Dry run** (example): r1, r2 queued → view 12. `fail r1` → queue `[r2]` → view `10 + 1 = 11`. `ok r2` → confirmed 11, queue empty → view 11.
guide.pitfalls: Clearing the queue on refetch loses clicks that are still in flight. Applying `ok` to the view as well as the confirmed data double-counts.
guide.follow_up: React 19's `useOptimistic(state, reducer)` implements exactly this replay model.

react-firestore-query.title: A Firestore-style query over an array
react-firestore-query.description:
Implement a small in-memory version of a Firestore collection query. `runQuery(docs, query)` returns the **ids** of
the matching documents in order. Every doc is `{ id, ...fields }`.

`query` may contain:

- `where`: a list of `[field, op, value]` filters, **all** of which must pass. `field` may be a dotted path such as
  `"stock.count"`. A document that lacks the field fails every filter on it.
  - `"=="`: strictly equal · `"!="`: field present and not strictly equal
  - `"<"`, `"<="`, `">"`, `">="`: only when the field value and `value` are **both numbers or both strings**; otherwise the filter fails
  - `"in"`: `value` is an array that contains the field value
  - `"array-contains"`: the field is an array that contains `value`
- `orderBy`: a list of `[field, "asc" | "desc"]`. Documents **missing any orderBy field are left out** (Firestore
  orders through an index, and a document without the field is not in that index). Later entries break ties of
  earlier ones. Remaining ties are broken by `id`, in the direction of the **last** orderBy entry. With no
  `orderBy`, sort by `id` ascending. Assume the values of an orderBy field are all numbers or all strings
- `startAfter`: a list of values, one per orderBy entry (a cursor). Keep only documents that come strictly **after**
  that position in the sort order (compare the orderBy fields only)
- `limit`: keep at most this many documents (applied last)

**Example:** `runQuery(docs, {where:[["city","==","Oslo"],["price",">=",20]], orderBy:[["price","desc"]], limit:2})`

guide.prereqs: Array `filter`/`sort`; lesson *Firestore and the Realtime Database*.
guide.intuition: A query is a pipeline: filter, order, skip to the cursor, cut to the limit. The Firestore-specific twists are that missing fields silently exclude documents and that every ordering ends with the document id as a tiebreaker.
hints: Write `get(doc, "a.b")` first and make it return `undefined` for anything missing.
Build one comparator that loops over the `orderBy` entries and falls back to the id.
For `startAfter`, reuse the comparison logic: keep a doc when its first differing orderBy value lies after the cursor's.
guide.brute_force: Sort first and filter afterwards, or apply the limit before ordering (second wrong solution): the top-2 of an unsorted list are not the top-2 by price.
guide.approach: **Dry run** (example): Oslo docs with price ≥ 20 → sort by price descending → first two ids.
guide.complexity: O(n · f + n log n) for n docs and f filters.
guide.pitfalls: JavaScript happily evaluates `"cheap" > 5` (false) and `undefined < 3` (false) but also `null >= 0` (true): always check types before range comparisons. Forgetting the id tiebreak makes pagination skip or repeat rows.
guide.follow_up: Real Firestore additionally requires a composite index for most multi-field queries and restricts which filter combinations are allowed.

react-rules-evaluator.title: Evaluate security rules
react-rules-evaluator.description:
Database security rules answer one question: may **this** user perform **this** operation on **this** path? Build an
evaluator for a small rule language (rules arrive as JSON, so there is nothing to parse).

`evaluate(rules, request)`

**Request:** `{ op, path, auth, data, existing }`. `op` is `"get" | "list" | "create" | "update" | "delete"`;
`auth` is `null` or `{ uid, token }`; `data` is the incoming document; `existing` the stored one (either may be `null`).

**Rule:** `{ match, allow, if }`

- `match` is a path pattern. `{name}` matches one segment and binds it; `{name=**}` (last segment only) matches
  **one or more** remaining segments and binds them joined by `/`; other segments must be equal. Segment counts must agree
- `allow` lists operations; `"read"` stands for `get` + `list` and `"write"` for `create` + `update` + `delete`
- `if` is a condition expression; a missing `if` means `true`

**Expressions**

- a string, number, boolean or `null` is a literal; an array is a list of expressions
- `{ var: "a.b.c" }` looks the path up in the scope `{ auth, data, existing, params }`. Stepping **through** `null`,
  a non-object, or a key that does not exist is an **error**. (The final value may be `null`.)
- `{ op, args }`: `"and"` / `"or"` evaluate left to right and stop early; every operand they evaluate must be a
  boolean, otherwise error. `"not"` needs a boolean. `"eq"` / `"neq"` use strict equality.
  `"lt" "lte" "gt" "gte"` need two numbers or two strings, otherwise error. `"in"`: `args[1]` must evaluate to an
  array (else error) and the result is whether it contains `args[0]`

A rule **grants** access when its path matches, its `allow` covers the operation and its condition evaluates to
exactly `true`. An error means that rule does not grant. Access is denied unless some rule grants it.

Return `{ allowed, matched, granted }`: `matched` holds the indexes of rules whose path and operation matched,
`granted` the indexes that granted.

guide.prereqs: Recursion over expression trees; lesson *Security rules*.
guide.intuition: Three independent pieces: a path matcher that produces bindings, an operation check, and a tiny interpreter. Rules are OR-ed together, and anything unexpected (a missing field, a wrong type) counts as 'no' for that rule only.
hints: Write `matchPath(pattern)` returning a params object or `null`.
The interpreter is one recursive function: literal, array, `var`, operator. Throw on every error case.
Wrap each rule's condition in `try/catch`; a throw means the rule does not grant.
guide.brute_force: Evaluate with JavaScript truthiness and no errors (the wrong solution). Then `undefined !== null` makes 'auth is not null' checks pass on missing data, `"50" >= 0` passes a string where a number was required, and unauthenticated users slip through, which is the classic way real rule sets leak.
guide.approach: **Dry run** `update /posts/p1`, `auth: null`: rule 2 matches path and op; `auth.uid` steps through `null` → error → not granted. Rule 5 (`/{path=**}`) matches; `auth.token.roles` errors → not granted. Denied, `matched: [2, 5]`.
guide.pitfalls: Letting `{name=**}` match zero segments; treating truthy non-booleans as true; aborting the whole evaluation when one rule errors; forgetting that rules never *revoke* access another rule granted.
guide.follow_up: Real Firestore rules add functions, `get()` lookups of other documents and `request.resource.data` validation.

react-route-guard.title: Role-based route guard
react-route-guard.description:
Before rendering a page, a protected-route component decides what to do with the visitor. Write
`guardRoute(route, session)`.

`route`: `{ path, public?, guestOnly?, requireVerified?, roles? }` · `session`: `{ status, user }` where `status` is
`"loading"` (the auth library has not yet reported whether someone is signed in), `"anonymous"` or
`"authenticated"`, and `user` is `null` or `{ roles: [...], emailVerified }`.

Apply the **first** rule that fits and return `{ action, to }` (`to` is `null` unless redirecting):

1. `route.public` → `render`
2. status `"loading"` → `wait` (show a spinner; redirecting now would kick out users who are in fact signed in)
3. `route.guestOnly` (sign-in / sign-up pages): authenticated → `redirect` to `"/"`; anonymous → `render`
4. anonymous → `redirect` to `"/signin?next="` + `encodeURIComponent(route.path)`
5. `route.requireVerified` and the email is not verified → `redirect` to `"/verify-email"`
6. `route.roles` is a non-empty list and the user has none of those roles → `redirect` to `"/forbidden"`
7. otherwise → `render`

**Example:** `guardRoute({path:"/admin/users", roles:["admin"]}, {status:"anonymous", user:null})` →
`{action:"redirect", to:"/signin?next=%2Fadmin%2Fusers"}`

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Sessions, protected routes and roles*.
guide.intuition: A guard is an ordered checklist. The order encodes priority: 'we do not know yet' must come before 'not signed in', and 'who are you' before 'what may you do'.
hints: Return early for each rule, in the listed order.
There are three session states, not two: handle `loading` explicitly.
`roles.some(r => user.roles.includes(r))` expresses 'has at least one of'.
guide.brute_force: A boolean `isLoggedIn`. On page refresh the app renders once before the auth library answers, so a signed-in user is bounced to the sign-in page and loses their place.
guide.approach: **Dry run** (example): not public; not loading; not guest-only; anonymous → redirect with the encoded path.
guide.pitfalls: Not encoding the `next` parameter (a path containing `&` or `?` gets cut off). Treating an empty `roles` list as 'nobody allowed'. Remember this guard is for user experience only: real enforcement is in the database rules.
guide.follow_up: Validate `next` after sign-in so it only ever points inside your own site (open-redirect protection).

react-entity-cache.title: Normalise nested data into an entity cache
react-entity-cache.description:
An API returns posts with their author and comments nested inside. Storing that as-is duplicates each user many
times, so renaming one user means hunting down every copy. A *normalised* store keeps each entity once, in a table
keyed by id, and links entities by id.

`normalizePosts(posts)` receives

```
[{ id, title, author: { id, name, ... }, comments: [{ id, text, author: { id, name, ... } }] }]
```

(`comments` may be missing) and returns three tables, each `{ byId, allIds }`:

- `users`: every author found (of posts and comments)
- `posts`: each post with `author` replaced by `authorId` and `comments` replaced by `commentIds` (`[]` when missing)
- `comments`: each comment with `author` replaced by `authorId`

Rules: `allIds` lists ids in **first-seen** order without duplicates (for each post: its author first, then the
post, then each comment's author followed by the comment). When the same id appears again, **shallow-merge** the new
fields over the stored ones (later data wins). All other fields are kept as they are. Do not modify the input.

guide.prereqs: Destructuring with rest; lesson *Context and global state* (state shape).
guide.intuition: Treat the response like rows arriving for three database tables. One `upsert(table, entity)` helper does all the work; the loop only decides which table each piece belongs to and swaps nested objects for ids.
hints: Write `upsert` first: push the id if it is new, then merge.
Destructure `author` and `comments` out of the post; the rest are the post's own fields.
Follow the stated visiting order so `allIds` comes out right.
guide.brute_force: Keep the nested array and search it on every update: O(posts × comments) per change and duplicated users that drift apart.
guide.approach: **Dry run** (first test): upsert user u1; post p1 `{title, authorId:u1, commentIds:[c1,c2]}`; user u2, comment c1; user u1 again (merge, no new id), comment c2.
guide.pitfalls: Pushing ids twice; replacing instead of merging (a comment author with fewer fields wipes the fuller profile); leaving the nested `author` object inside the stored post.
guide.follow_up: Reading back ('denormalising') for one screen is a selector: `ids.map(id => byId[id])`. Firestore and the Realtime Database push you towards the same flat, id-linked shape.

react-snapshot-changes.title: Apply realtime snapshot changes
react-snapshot-changes.description:
A realtime listener does not have to hand you the whole list each time. Firestore's `snapshot.docChanges()` reports
what changed since the previous snapshot, with the positions involved. Write `applyChanges(list, changes)` that
applies them **in order** to a copy of `list` (an array of `{ id, ... }`) and returns the new array.

| change | meaning |
|---|---|
| `{type:"added", doc, newIndex}` | insert `doc` at `newIndex` |
| `{type:"removed", doc, oldIndex}` | remove the element at `oldIndex` |
| `{type:"modified", doc, oldIndex, newIndex}` | remove the element at `oldIndex`, then insert the new `doc` at `newIndex` (the indexes differ when the change affected the sort position) |

Indexes always refer to the list as it is at the moment that change is applied. Do not modify `list`.

**Example:** list `[{id:"a",n:1},{id:"b",n:2}]`, changes
`[{type:"modified", doc:{id:"a",n:9}, oldIndex:0, newIndex:1}, {type:"added", doc:{id:"c",n:0}, newIndex:0}]`
→ `[{id:"c",n:0},{id:"b",n:2},{id:"a",n:9}]`

guide.prereqs: `Array.prototype.splice`; lesson *Firestore and the Realtime Database*.
guide.intuition: Each change is a remove, an insert, or both. `modified` is 'remove from the old seat, sit down in the new seat'.
hints: Copy the list once at the start.
Do the removal before the insertion for `modified`.
Two `if` statements cover all three types.
guide.brute_force: Throw the list away and rebuild it from `snapshot.docs` each time. That is fine for small lists (and is what most apps do); `docChanges` matters for animations and very long lists.
guide.approach: **Dry run** (example): remove index 0 → `[b]`; insert `a(9)` at 1 → `[b, a]`; insert `c` at 0 → `[c, b, a]`.
guide.pitfalls: Appending added docs ignores the query's ordering. Inserting before removing shifts the old index.
guide.follow_up: The first snapshot of a listener reports every existing document as `added`.
